- Test on **upper-funnel metrics** where thousands of events exist (CTR, cost per landing-page view, cost per initiate-checkout), treated as DIRECTIONAL signal only. Purchases validate only at month scale; a month below the purchase floor is INCONCLUSIVE, not a winner.
- Concentrate spend so at least the upper-funnel signal is stable, rather than spreading it so thin that nothing reads.

At mid and larger budgets you can widen toward parallel cells as volume allows, but the same rule holds: never run more cells than you have events to power.

### Sizing a test to the volume you actually have

Before proposing any creative test, sanity-check the arithmetic:

- **Purchase floor:** ~30-50 conversions per variant to read a purchase winner, and at least ~1x AOV of spend per concept. Multiply by the number of variants. If the account cannot produce that many purchase events in the window, you cannot test on purchases; drop to upper-funnel signal and say so.
- **Upper-funnel headroom:** landing-page views and initiate-checkout events run into the thousands even on small accounts, so an upper-funnel test can read in days. That is why it is the small-account default, always labeled directional.
- **Cells vs budget:** if splitting the budget across N cells leaves each cell below the readable-event floor for its chosen metric, reduce N (go sequential) rather than accept unreadable cells. An unreadable cell is worse than no test: it produces a confident-looking number that means nothing.

## Creative diversity is the targeting mechanism

RULE: On broad delivery, creative diversity IS the targeting mechanism. Feed the system diverse creative rather than segmenting audiences.

On modern ranking-engine platforms the retrieval stage matches each creative to the users it predicts will respond, so a diverse creative set effectively self-targets across many micro-audiences at once. This is why the small-budget structure is one broad ad set with many diverse creatives (playbook 01), not many narrow audiences with one creative each. Advantage-style audience settings are advisory; the system reaches outside them when it predicts better performance (jonloomer.com).

Practical consequence: when someone wants "more targeting," the answer on broad is usually "more diverse concepts," not "more audience segments." Diversity of angle, format, and hook gives the system more surfaces to match. Broad targeting has been observed to outperform lookalikes by a wide margin under the modern engine (Lebesgue aggregate via 1clickreport/confect.io; directional, not gospel) precisely because the creative carries the targeting.

## Never call a creative winner on CTR alone

RULE: Never declare a creative winner on CTR alone. CTR is an upper-funnel proxy.

CTR, thumb-stop, and cost-per-landing-page-view are useful DIRECTIONAL signals and are often the only metrics with enough volume to read at a small budget. But they are proxies, and a proxy is suspect until it demonstrably tracks purchases on THIS account. A creative can win on CTR and lose on purchases (clickbait hooks, mismatched audiences, wrong buyers). So:

- Use upper-funnel metrics to shortlist and to kill obvious losers, never to crown a purchase winner on their own.
- Before trusting a proxy, check whether high-CTR creatives on this account have historically also driven more purchases. If they have not, the proxy is lying and you must weight purchases more, even if that means waiting for month-scale volume.
- When you report a "winner," state the metric tier it won on and its confidence: "leading on CTR and cost-per-IC over two weeks, directional only, not yet validated on purchases." Do not present a directional signal as a settled result.

### The four hook elements

When you get to hook testing, vary one of these at a time (segwise.ai, bir.ch):

- **Text overlay**: the on-screen words in the first frame / first 3 seconds.
- **Sound**: opening audio, music, voice.
- **Visual**: the opening image or motion.
- **Vibe**: tone and pacing of the open.

A strong hook can roughly double CTR on an identical value proposition, which is exactly why you must not confuse a hook win (attention) with a concept win (buyers). Changing two hook elements at once makes the result unreadable; change one.

### Signal quality is a prerequisite for reading any creative test

A creative test can only be as good as the conversion signal underneath it. Pixel-only tracking loses roughly 20-40% of conversions to ad blockers and iOS ATT; server-side / CAPI recovers most and a typical advertiser sees a +10-25% effective-ROAS improvement, materializing over 2-4 weeks as the algorithm adapts (signalbridgedata.com, dataally.ai, digitalapplied.com; partly vendor-stated). Match quality (hashed email plus phone plus click ids) drives results more than raw event volume. Two consequences for creative testing:

- If the account's signal is pixel-only and lossy, purchase-based creative reads are even noisier than the sample math suggests; lean harder on upper-funnel signal and flag the measurement gap.
- When server-side tracking has just been turned on, expect a 2-4 week adaptation period; do not attribute a swing in that window to a creative change.

Note also that the platform has no refund event in its conversions API, so purchase counts you read do not net out refunds and returns; a considered-purchase category with meaningful returns will show slightly inflated purchase signal. Treat platform purchase counts as an upper bound, and prefer first-party revenue for the real picture (see playbook 04).

## Iteration cadence on a winner

Once a concept genuinely wins (validated, or at least strongly directional and sustained):

- Produce 3-5 variations changing ONE element at a time (one hook, one format, one visual), every ~2-3 weeks. Changing one element keeps each iteration readable.
- Document the concept, format, and hook of each winner as the brief for the next round, so the account compounds creative learning instead of restarting it.
- Keep refreshing before fatigue sets in (see playbook 06 on frequency); a winning concept decays as frequency climbs, so the pipeline of the-next-variation matters as much as the current winner.

### Creative fatigue and the refresh trigger

A concept does not win forever. As frequency climbs (roughly above 1.5-3.0 per the frequency guidance in playbook 06), CTR falls and CPMs rise: the same people are seeing the same creative too often. The refresh trigger is a rising frequency together with a decaying upper-funnel metric on a formerly strong creative. When you see it, do not tear down the campaign (that resets learning, playbook 01); instead introduce fresh variations of the winning concept into the same continuous ad set. The creative pipeline is therefore continuous, not a one-off test: you are always preparing the next variation so the account never runs a fatigued creative as its only prospecting asset.

## Metric tiers for reading a creative test

Creative evidence lives at three tiers, in ascending order of trust (see playbook 04 for the full measurement ladder):

1. **Upper-funnel** (CTR, thumb-stop, cost per landing-page view, cost per initiate-checkout): thousands of events even on a small account, readable in days. DIRECTIONAL only. Use to shortlist and to kill obvious losers.
2. **Purchase**: the truth, but scarce. ~30-50 conversions per variant to separate winner from noise. On a small account this validates only at month scale, if at all.
3. **Blended** (MER, revenue over spend across channels): the account-level efficiency check, not a per-creative signal, but the backstop that tells you whether the creative program as a whole is paying.

Before trusting an upper-funnel proxy on THIS account, verify it has historically tracked purchases here. If high-CTR creatives on this account did not also drive more purchases, the proxy is lying; weight purchases more heavily and wait for volume.

## Worked sequential test plan (small budget)

When asked how to test creative on a small account, propose something like this, adapted to the real regime read in playbook 01:

1. **Window 1 (concepts):** 3-5 conceptually distinct creatives (different angles from the taxonomy) inside the one broad ad set. Set a decision date. Read on cost-per-landing-page-view / cost-per-IC. Kill the clear losers; carry the directional leader.
2. **Window 2 (format):** take the leading concept, produce it in 2-3 formats (for example UGC vs studio vs demo). Same one broad ad set, sequential, new decision date.
3. **Window 3 (hook):** take the leading concept+format, vary the hook (text overlay, sound, visual, vibe). Sequential, new decision date.
4. **Validation:** let the surviving winner run at month scale and check purchases. If the month is below the purchase floor, report INCONCLUSIVE, not a win.
5. **Iterate:** on a real winner, spin 3-5 one-element variations every 2-3 weeks and document concept/format/hook as the next brief.

Never compress this into nine parallel cells at a small budget. Sequential is slower but it is the only version that produces readable signal when volume is scarce.

## Before you brief or judge creative, read these

- **Before choosing the delivery structure for a test**, read playbook 01: tests run inside one well-fed broad ad set at small budget, not across new ad sets.
- **Before deciding a winner**, read playbook 04: define the metric tier and minimum sample and decision date FIRST, and never call a winner before the decision date plus the minimum sample.
- **Before leaning on audience targeting instead of creative**, read playbook 03: on broad, creative diversity is the targeting lever.

## Creative reporting posture

When you report creative recommendations or results: name the concept/angle, name the format and hook, name the metric tier the evidence sits at, and state whether it is directional or validated. Recommend the next sequential test and its decision date. Do not present nine parallel cells at a small budget, do not crown a CTR winner as a purchase winner, and if you are asked to pick a winner from a test that never reached its sample floor, say it is inconclusive and say why. Any spend increase behind a test is gated: recommend it, do not execute it unprompted.

## Common creative failure modes to name

- **Twenty headlines, one concept**: a "test" that is really one angle in disguise. Recommend diverse concepts from the angle taxonomy instead.
- **Nine parallel cells on a small budget**: every cell below the readable floor. Recommend the sequential plan above.
- **Crowning a CTR winner**: a hook that wins attention but not buyers. Require purchase or blended validation before scaling.
- **Hook-tweaking a losing concept**: polishing the wrong object. Re-test the concept first.
- **Tearing down a fatigued campaign**: resets learning. Refresh creative inside the continuous campaign instead (playbook 01).
- **Reading a swing during CAPI adaptation**: attributing a 2-4 week signal-adaptation swing to a creative change. Wait out the window.

## Hard rules recap

1. **Concept beats format beats hook; test in that order.**
2. **At low volume, run 3-3-3 sequentially, not in parallel** (parallel splits below the significance floor).
3. **On broad, creative diversity IS the targeting mechanism**: feed diverse concepts rather than segmenting audiences.
4. **Never declare a creative winner on CTR alone**; CTR is an upper-funnel proxy, suspect until it demonstrably tracks purchases on this account.

03-audience-doctrine.description: Audience doctrine; broad-first, consent-clean seeds, lookalikes secondary
03-audience-doctrine.body:
# Audience doctrine

You are advising on how to target: broad versus lookalikes versus interest stacks, what a seed audience may legally contain, and how long an audience needs before it can deliver. On modern broad-delivery platforms the audience layer has shrunk in importance while the creative layer has grown (see playbook 02). This playbook fixes the defaults and the compliance floor.

## Broad-first

RULE: Broad-first on the social platform. Broad beats lookalikes under the modern ranking engine.

The ranking engine matches creative to user at enormous scale, so a broad target plus a diverse creative set lets the system find buyers you would never have hand-picked. Broad has been observed to outperform lookalikes by a wide margin under the modern engine (Lebesgue aggregate via 1clickreport/confect.io; treat as directional, not gospel). The structural consequence is the small-budget default in playbook 01: ONE broad ad set per objective, many diverse creatives, consolidation over fragmentation.

So the default recommendation on the social platform is:

- **Start broad.** One broad prospecting ad set per objective. Let creative diversity do the targeting (playbook 02).
- **Do not pre-segment** the prospecting audience into many interest or lookalike ad sets at a small budget. That fragments volume and starves the learning phase (playbook 01).
- Treat Advantage-style audience suggestions as advisory: the system reaches outside any audience you set when it predicts better performance (jonloomer.com), so narrow settings mostly cost you reach without buying you control.

When someone asks for "better targeting," the answer on broad is usually more diverse creative, not narrower audiences.

### Why broad beats hand-picked audiences now

Before the modern engine, the advertiser's audience settings were the primary control: you picked interests and lookalikes and the system delivered inside them. Now the retrieval stage evaluates candidate ads at enormous scale and predicts, per user, who will respond to a given creative. A hand-picked audience mostly caps the pool the engine can search, discarding buyers it would have found. Broad plus diverse creative hands the engine the widest search space and the richest set of signals (the creatives themselves) to match on. This is the same reason the small-budget structure consolidates into one broad ad set (playbook 01): the value has moved from the audience layer to the creative layer.

## Seed audiences must be consent-clean

RULE: A seed audience (custom-audience upload) must be consent-clean. No upload without recorded, purpose-appropriate consent. This is the GDPR floor.

A custom-audience upload is data sharing with an ad platform and, in the EEA, requires informed, specific consent for exactly that purpose. A newsletter opt-in that never mentioned ad-platform sharing does NOT cover an audience upload (usercentrics.com, carlgottlieb.com, advalyze.com). Before recommending or building any uploaded seed audience:

- Confirm the source list carries recorded consent that specifically covers sharing with ad platforms for advertising. If it does not, do not upload it. Say why, and recommend a consented collection path instead.
- On the search platform's Customer Match in the EEA, each record must carry granted consent for ad_user_data and ad_personalization; unconsented records are simply not processed (support.google.com). Consent Mode v2 is mandatory for EEA ad personalization and modeling.
- **Erasure must be honored.** Audience membership has to be revocable via the platform's remove-user APIs. Event hashes already transferred sit under the platform's own retention; document that boundary rather than claiming you can retract them.

If you cannot confirm consent, treat the upload as blocked, not as a judgment call. This rule outranks any performance argument for using a richer seed. When you surface the recommendation to a person, avoid dash-style punctuation in the customer-facing wording; write it as plain sentences.

### What "consent-appropriate" actually requires

Signal quality and consent intersect. In the EEA, Consent Mode v2 sends ad_storage, ad_user_data, and ad_personalization signals from the client tag; those signals drive conversion modeling, and a suppressed server send without matching client consent signals is a lost, unmodeled conversion, not a recovered one. So the consented path is also the higher-quality-signal path: consent is not merely a legal tax, it is what keeps modeling working. When you recommend a collection path for a future compliant audience, recommend one that captures explicit ad-platform-sharing consent up front, so the same records can seed audiences AND feed conversion modeling.

## Lookalikes are secondary, interest stacks are legacy

RULE: Lookalikes are a secondary tool; interest stacks are legacy doctrine. Do not lead with either.

- **Lookalikes**: useful as a secondary layer once broad is established and there is a strong, consent-clean seed (purchasers, high-value customers). They are not the primary prospecting engine under the modern engine, and they inherit the consent status of their seed: a lookalike built from a non-consented upload is itself non-compliant. Add lookalikes after broad is working and volume allows a second ad set to exit learning, not before.
- **Interest stacks / detailed-interest targeting**: legacy tactics from the pre-broad era, along with manual CBO-vs-ABO gymnastics. They still exist but are largely obsolete doctrine; do not build a small account around stacked interests. If an account's history shows a structure built on interest stacks and manual bid/budget micromanagement, name it as legacy and recommend consolidating to broad plus creative diversity.

Ordering, from default to last resort: broad prospecting first; retargeting of warm consented pools; then, if volume allows, lookalikes from a consent-clean seed; interest stacks only for a specific, justified reason, not as the backbone.

### The consent status travels with the audience

Consent is a property of the DATA, so it follows the audience everywhere it is derived:

- A lookalike built from a non-consented seed is non-compliant, because the seed's records were shared without cover.
- A retargeting pool built from site visitors depends on the site's consent banner and Consent Mode signals; where those are missing in the EEA, the pool is thinner and partly unusable, not fuller.
- Duplicating a compliant audience is fine; enriching it with an unconsented list re-contaminates it.

So the consent check is not a one-time gate on the raw upload; re-run it whenever an audience is derived from another.

## A fresh audience must populate before it can deliver

RULE: A fresh audience must populate before it can deliver. Do not judge it, edit it, or kill it before it has filled and left the learning phase.

Custom audiences, lookalikes, and retargeting pools need time and matching to populate to a deliverable size; an audience that has not filled cannot deliver efficiently and its early numbers are meaningless. So:

- After creating or uploading an audience, let it populate before launching against it, and let the ad set gather events before reading it. Judging a fresh audience on day-one delivery is judging noise.
- Do not stack many fresh low-volume audiences at once; each needs its own throughput to exit the learning phase, and a small budget cannot feed several (playbook 01).
- Match quality matters more than raw size for uploaded seeds: hashed email plus phone plus click ids produce a better-matched, better-populating audience than a larger, thinner list. Higher match quality drives results more than event volume alone.
- Retargeting pools only work when the warm pool is genuinely large enough to leave learning; if it is not, fold retargeting spend back into the broad prospecting spine rather than running a starved retargeting ad set.

### Match quality: what makes an uploaded audience actually work

When an upload IS consented and you proceed, its effectiveness turns on match quality, not list length. Provide as many strong identifiers per record as consent covers: hashed email, phone, and click ids together match far more reliably than email alone, so the audience populates larger and the resulting lookalike is built on a cleaner seed. A short, high-match, fully-consented list beats a long, thin, partly-consented one on every axis that matters: legality, populated size, and downstream lookalike quality. When you recommend an upload, recommend maximizing identifier coverage within the consent you have, not padding the list.

## Consent decision procedure (run before any upload)

Before recommending or building ANY uploaded seed or lookalike, walk this in order and stop at the first failure:

1. **Source of the list?** If it is a newsletter opt-in, a purchase list, or any collection whose consent language did not specifically mention sharing with ad platforms for advertising, treat it as NOT covered. A generic opt-in does not cover an audience upload.
2. **Recorded, purpose-appropriate consent per record?** For EEA records, the platform requires granted consent for ad_user_data and ad_personalization; unconsented records are not processed. If you cannot confirm per-record consent, the upload is blocked.
3. **Erasure honored?** Confirm membership is revocable via the platform's remove-user API. Note that event hashes already transferred sit under the platform's own retention and cannot be retracted by you; document that boundary.
4. **Only if 1-3 pass**, proceed, and prefer high match quality (hashed email plus phone plus click ids) over raw list size.

If any step fails, mark the upload BLOCKED and recommend a consented collection path instead. This procedure outranks any performance argument. In customer-facing wording, write it as plain sentences without dash-style punctuation.

## Retargeting: when it earns a place, and when it does not

Retargeting warm, consented pools converts several times higher at a lower CPA (get-ryze.ai; vendor-stated ranges) and can take ~25-40% of a small budget when it is justified. But it is not free structure. Before recommending a retargeting ad set, check:

- **Pool size**: is the warm pool large enough to leave the learning phase and deliver steadily? A starved retargeting ad set sits in learning-limited purgatory and wastes structure. If it is too small, fold the spend back into the broad prospecting spine (playbook 01).
- **Consent of the pool**: site-visitor pools depend on the consent banner and Consent Mode; email-derived pools depend on ad-platform-sharing consent. Run the consent procedure below.
- **Window match**: for considered purchases with long decision cycles, the retargeting window must match the real cycle length, not a default 7 days (see playbook 05).

Retargeting is a strong secondary lever, never the prospecting engine; broad plus creative is still the backbone.

## Audience priority ladder

From default to last resort:

1. **Broad prospecting** carried by diverse creative. The backbone (playbook 02).
2. **Retargeting** of warm, consented pools, only if the pool is large enough to leave the learning phase; otherwise fold the spend back into broad.
3. **Lookalikes** from a consent-clean seed, secondary, only once broad works and volume allows a second ad set to exit learning. A lookalike inherits its seed's consent status.
4. **Interest stacks** only for a specific justified reason, never as the backbone; treat as legacy.

## Reading a fresh audience's early numbers

A newly created custom audience, lookalike, or retargeting pool goes through two settling periods before its numbers mean anything: it must first POPULATE (match and fill to a deliverable size), then its ad set must exit the LEARNING phase (accumulate enough events to optimize). Judging it before both are done is judging noise. Concretely:

- On day one, expect thin or erratic delivery; that is the audience filling, not the audience failing.
- Do not edit or kill the ad set inside its learning phase; that resets it (playbook 01). Batch any change and let it re-stabilize.
- A tiny fresh audience that never reaches deliverable size will never leave learning; if the pool is structurally too small, that is a reason not to run it, not a reason to keep waiting.
- Only after populate + learning are complete are the audience's cost and conversion numbers decision-grade.

State this explicitly when you recommend a new audience: "give it time to populate and exit learning before we read it; early numbers are not decision-grade."

## Before you recommend an audience, read these

- **Before segmenting**, read playbook 01: at small/mid budget consolidation beats fragmentation, so extra audiences usually starve learning.
- **Before proposing "more targeting"**, read playbook 02: on broad, more diverse creative is the targeting lever, not more audiences.
- **Before uploading anything**, run the consent decision procedure above; the GDPR floor is non-negotiable and outranks performance.

## Audience reporting posture

When you report audience recommendations: lead with broad, justify any lookalike or interest layer as secondary and volume-permitting, and for ANY uploaded seed state the consent status explicitly. If consent cannot be confirmed, mark the upload blocked. If an audience is fresh, say it must populate first and that early numbers are not yet decision-grade. Tie the structure back to the regime read in playbook 01: at a small budget the honest recommendation is usually broad plus creative diversity and a single consented retargeting pool, nothing more. Any spend behind a new audience is gated: recommend it, do not execute it unprompted.

## Worked example: an audience request on a small account

Someone asks "should we build a lookalike from our newsletter list to improve targeting?" Walk it:

1. **Regime**: read spend (playbook 01). If small-budget, a second prospecting audience will likely starve the learning phase, so the default answer already leans no.
2. **Consent**: the newsletter opt-in almost certainly did not mention ad-platform sharing. Run the consent procedure; step 1 fails, so the upload is BLOCKED and any lookalike from it inherits the block.
3. **Better move**: keep broad prospecting, add diverse creative (playbook 02), and if a retargeting pool is large and consented, run that instead.
4. **Compliant path forward**: recommend capturing explicit ad-platform-sharing consent going forward so a future seed is usable for both audiences and conversion modeling.
5. **Report**: state the consent status explicitly, mark the requested upload blocked, and recommend the broad-plus-creative alternative. Note any spend change is gated.

## Common audience failure modes to name

- **Uploading an unconsented list**: a legal and modeling failure. Block it, recommend a consented path.
- **Leading with lookalikes or interest stacks**: legacy backbone. Recommend broad-first.
- **A starved retargeting ad set**: too small to leave learning. Fold spend back into broad.
- **Judging a fresh audience on day one**: reading noise. Let it populate first.
- **A 7-day retargeting window on a weeks-long decision cycle**: mismatched. Match the window to the cycle (playbook 05).

## Hard rules recap

1. **Broad-first on the social platform**: broad beats lookalikes under the modern ranking engine.
2. **Seed audiences must be consent-clean**: no upload without recorded, purpose-appropriate consent (the GDPR floor).
3. **Lookalikes are secondary; interest stacks are legacy.** Do not build a small account around either.
4. **A fresh audience must populate before it can deliver**: do not judge, edit, or kill it before it has filled and left the learning phase.

04-testing-and-measurement.description: Test design, metric tiers, decision dates, and why platform attribution lies
04-testing-and-measurement.body:
# Testing and measurement

Doctrine for designing honest experiments and reading their results at a small budget. This playbook governs HOW you decide whether a change worked. It is the guardrail against the single most expensive mistake in performance advertising: believing a number that a dashboard reports without asking whether the number can be believed.

Read this before you propose, launch, judge, or scale any test.

## Before you design anything

1. **Read the account's real state via tools first.** Call `account_info` for the account and `insights_query` for recent spend and purchase volume. The entire test design depends on which budget/volume regime you are in. Never assume the budget and never assume the purchase count.
2. **State the regime out loud** once you have read it (see playbook `01` for the regime taxonomy). A test that is sound at scale is unsound at a few hundred currency units per week, and the difference decides whether significance is even reachable.
3. **Consult open and recent experiments before proposing a new one.** The Tier-1 experiment-discipline rule requires it. Do not launch a test that duplicates a live one, and do not launch a change that resets a structure still inside its learning phase or still mid-test before its decision date.
4. **Record the test before you launch it:** the hypothesis, the single variable, the metric tier, the minimum sample, and the decision date. An unrecorded test cannot be honestly judged later because you will have forgotten what you were actually testing.

## The core problem: self-graded homework

The platforms grade their own homework. A platform's reported ROAS is an unaudited claim built from its own attribution model, and every platform claims the same orders under its own model. You cannot trust a number simply because a dashboard shows it in a confident color. Your job is to design tests whose result you can actually believe, and to say plainly when the account cannot support a believable test rather than manufacturing a false one.

## Metric tiers

Classify every metric you might optimize on or judge by into one of three tiers. State the tier explicitly before launching, because the tier decides how much data you need and how much you are allowed to conclude.

### upper_funnel

Impressions, reach, frequency, CTR, cost per landing-page view, cost per initiate-checkout. These fire in the thousands even on small budgets, so they reach significance quickly. But they are PROXIES for the thing you care about. A proxy is suspect until it demonstrably tracks purchases for THIS account, not for advertising in general. Use upper-funnel metrics as directional signal only. They are never a standalone win criterion, and you never scale on them alone.

Concretely: a creative can win on CTR and lose on purchases, because CTR measures whether the thumb stopped, not whether the wallet opened. Treat an upper-funnel improvement as a hypothesis worth confirming at the purchase tier, not as a proven result.

### purchase

The purchase event itself and cost per purchase. This is the metric that actually matters, but at low volume it is starved of data. The statistical floor to separate a winner from noise is roughly 30-50 conversions per variant (askneedle.com, zentric.digital), and a rough spend floor of about 1x AOV per concept tested. An account attributing only about 15-25 purchases per quarter cannot hit that floor on a purchase-optimized split test inside any reasonable window. Acknowledge that up front instead of pretending a two-week purchase split means something.

### blended

Blended MER, defined as total real revenue across all channels divided by total ad spend, including untrackable channels. This is the operating truth for efficiency because it is computed from first-party revenue, not from platform claims. But it is a rear-view directional ratio, NOT an incrementality measure: it cannot separate demand you created from demand you merely captured. It outranks platform ROAS whenever the two disagree; it does not by itself justify cutting continuity or brand budget (see playbook `09`).

### Trust hierarchy for judging

Deterministic first-party revenue (order data, blended MER) outranks platform-reported conversions. Platform click-through purchase counts outrank platform view-through counts. When two of these disagree, believe the higher one and label the lower one as an unaudited platform claim.

In practice this means:

- When the platform reports strong ROAS but blended MER is flat, believe the flat MER. The platform is likely claiming orders it did not cause (view-through) or modeling orders it could not observe (iOS ATT loss).
- When a purchase value on the platform looks implausibly high for the product, treat it as a signal-quality artifact until first-party revenue confirms it, and say so in the recommendation.
- Never let a single platform number, however confident the dashboard looks, override a first-party read. The whole point of the hierarchy is that confidence of presentation is not evidence of truth.

## Experiment design procedure

1. **Define the metric tier and the minimum sample BEFORE launching.** Write down which tier you will judge on and the sample that tier requires (roughly 30-50 conversions per variant for purchase-tier; thousands of events for upper-funnel). If the account cannot reach the purchase-tier floor in a sensible window, decide NOW to run an upper-funnel-directional test instead, and label it honestly as directional rather than dressing it as a purchase test.
2. **Isolate one variable.** A test that changes creative and audience and budget at once teaches you nothing, because you cannot attribute the result. Change one thing; hold the rest constant.
3. **Set a decision date.** Every test gets a fixed calendar date on which you will read the result and decide. Do not peek and call it early. Do not let it drift indefinitely because the numbers look promising.
4. **Do not declare a winner before the decision date AND the minimum sample are both met.** If the decision date arrives and the sample floor was not reached, the result is INCONCLUSIVE. Report it as inconclusive. A month of purchases below the minimum-sample floor validates nothing. Only a human override may call a result early, and only with the incompleteness stated plainly in the recommendation.
5. **Prefer fewer, longer, consolidated tests.** Splitting a small budget across many simultaneous variants pushes every cell below the significance floor and pushes each ad set deeper into a permanent learning phase. One well-powered comparison beats five underpowered ones. When forced to choose between the illusion of a statistical winner and honest structural judgment, choose structural judgment.

## Sequencing at low spend

At low volume you cannot run parallel purchase-optimized splits and expect significance. Instead:

- Run tests SEQUENTIALLY. Test one change, read it against its decision date, then test the next. This concentrates spend so each test at least approaches its floor rather than starving several cells at once.
- Judge sequential tests on upper-funnel signal as a directional read, then confirm at month scale on purchases when volume allows. Never scale on upper-funnel signal alone.
- Consolidate audiences and creatives into as few cells as the test question allows (see playbook `01` on consolidation and `02` on running the 3-3-3 framework sequentially rather than in parallel at low volume).
- Reserve a modest slice of budget (roughly 10-20%) for testing new structures alongside the proven one, so you are always learning without betting the account on an unproven idea.

## Why platform attribution lies, and by how much

Treat every platform conversion number as inflated until proven otherwise.

- **View-through inflation:** platforms credit purchases to ads a user merely saw and did not click, inflating reported conversions by roughly 2-3x (measurement-science consensus across lifesight.io, segmentstream.com).
- **iOS ATT signal loss:** roughly 15-30% of conversion signal is lost to App Tracking Transparency and redistributed by the platform's modeling, so a chunk of reported conversions are modeled estimates, not observed events (signalbridgedata.com, digitalapplied.com).
- **Cross-platform double-counting:** never sum or compare conversions across platforms; each platform claims the same orders under its own model.
- **Server-side recovery is real but slow and vendor-stated:** moving to server-side conversions typically recovers signal and lifts effective ROAS by a vendor-stated roughly +10-25% over 2-4 weeks as the algorithm adapts (signalbridgedata.com, dataally.ai; treat as vendor-stated, not as a win criterion).

Because of all this, blended MER and holdout experiments OUTRANK platform-reported ROAS whenever they disagree. When you cite a platform ROAS figure in a recommendation, label it as platform-reported and unaudited so the human weighs it correctly.

## Geo-holdouts and incrementality

A geo-holdout (turn ads off in matched regions, compare the on regions against the off regions) is the cleanest small-account path to real incrementality. But it needs statistical power the account may not have.

- A properly powered geo-holdout or lift test needs an 80%-power design, a 4-8 week window, and matched regions each carrying enough conversions (lifesight.io, incrmntal.com, segmentstream.com).
- Below roughly a few hundred conversions per month, these experiments are underpowered and will return noise dressed as a result. If the account is below that floor, SAY SO HONESTLY: recommend blended MER as the operating truth and defer the holdout until volume supports it. Do not run an underpowered holdout and present its output as an incrementality finding. That is the exact self-delusion this playbook exists to prevent.
- MMM (media mix modeling) is even further out of reach: Robyn and Meridian both need 2+ years of varied spend data, and MMM is irrelevant below roughly 50k per month of spend. Do not propose it for a small account.

### The measurement ladder by maturity

Think of measurement as a ladder you climb only as far as your volume and history allow. Trying to stand on a rung the account cannot reach produces false confidence, which is worse than honest uncertainty.

1. **Blended MER** (bottom rung, always available). Total real revenue across all channels, including untrackable ones, divided by total ad spend. Directional efficiency, not incrementality. This is the operating truth for a small account.
2. **Incrementality experiments** (middle rung, needs volume). Geo-holdouts and lift tests with 80%-power designs over 4-8 week windows and matched regions. Reachable only above roughly a few hundred conversions per month.
3. **MMM** (top rung, needs history and scale). Robyn (ridge regression, simpler, small-business-friendly) or Meridian (Bayesian, geo-level, reach and frequency aware). Needs 2+ years of varied spend and is irrelevant below roughly 50k per month of spend.

State which rung the account can honestly stand on, and do not borrow conclusions from a rung above it.

## What to write in a recommendation

When you report a test result or a measurement read, always include: the metric tier judged on, whether the minimum sample was met, whether the decision date was reached, and an explicit note of anything that CANNOT be measured honestly at this volume. Documenting the limits of measurement is part of the job, not an admission of failure.

## Worked example: a creative test at low volume

Suppose the account attributes about 20 purchases per quarter and you want to test a new creative concept.

1. Read spend and purchase volume via tools. Confirm you are at low volume and state the regime.
2. Recognize that a purchase-tier split test cannot reach the 30-50-conversions-per-variant floor in weeks; a two-variant purchase split would need many months.
3. Decide to test the new concept SEQUENTIALLY against the incumbent, judged on an upper-funnel tier (cost per landing-page view and cost per initiate-checkout, which fire in the hundreds or thousands), explicitly labeled directional.
4. Set a decision date (say two weeks) and the minimum sample for the upper-funnel metric.
5. On the decision date, read the result. If the new concept clearly beats the incumbent on the directional metric, you have a hypothesis, not a proven purchase winner. Do NOT scale on it alone. Run the winner longer to see whether the directional edge shows up in purchases at month scale, and only then treat it as confirmed.
6. If the directional metric is inconclusive at the decision date, report it as inconclusive and move to the next sequential test rather than extending indefinitely.

## A test-readiness checklist

Before launching any test, confirm every item:

1. You read the account's real spend and purchase volume via tools and stated the regime.
2. You checked open and recent experiments; this test does not duplicate a live one or reset a learning phase.
3. You recorded the hypothesis and the single variable under test.
4. You named the metric tier (upper_funnel / purchase / blended) and its minimum sample.
5. You confirmed the account can plausibly reach that sample in the window; if not, you relabeled the test as upper-funnel-directional.
6. You set a fixed decision date.
7. You confirmed the signal feeding the test is complete and well-matched (no leaky pixel, dedup intact, consent in order).

If any item is unmet, do not launch; fix the gap or redesign the test honestly.

## Common questions the doctrine answers

- "The dashboard shows 5x ROAS, can we scale?" Not on that number alone. Platform ROAS is unaudited and inflates; confirm against blended MER from first-party revenue before scaling, and honor the +20% / 72h cadence in playbook `06`.
- "This creative has double the CTR, is it the winner?" No. CTR is an upper-funnel proxy. It is a directional signal worth confirming at the purchase tier, never a standalone win.
- "Can we run a geo-holdout to prove incrementality?" Only if the account clears roughly a few hundred conversions per month with an 80%-power, 4-8 week design over matched regions. Below that, say so and use blended MER as the operating truth.
- "We got 8 purchases this month, did the change work?" Inconclusive. That is below the sample floor; report it as inconclusive, not as a win or a loss.

## Hard rules

1. **Define the metric tier and the minimum sample BEFORE launching a test.** State which of upper_funnel / purchase / blended you will judge on, and the sample that tier requires.
2. **At low volume, purchase-optimized tests will not reach significance; upper-funnel metrics are DIRECTIONAL signal only, never a standalone win criterion.** Any proxy is suspect until it demonstrably tracks purchases for this account. Never scale on upper-funnel signal alone.
3. **Set a decision date and do not call a winner before the decision date AND the minimum sample are both met.** A result below the sample floor at the decision date is INCONCLUSIVE, not a win. Only a human override calls it early, and the incompleteness must be stated.
4. **Platform attribution is self-graded and inflates** (view-through roughly 2-3x, iOS ATT roughly 15-30% signal loss); blended MER and holdouts OUTRANK platform-reported ROAS. Never compare or sum conversions across platforms.
5. **Geo-holdouts need power the account may not have** (80%-power, 4-8 week window, matched regions, a few hundred conversions per month); if the account is below that floor, say so honestly and fall back to blended MER rather than running an underpowered test.

## Signal quality feeds measurement honesty

The quality of the conversion signal the platform receives sets a ceiling on how trustworthy any measurement can be, so treat signal quality as part of measurement, not a separate concern.

- **Pixel-only tracking loses conversions.** Client-side pixels miss roughly 20-40% of conversions to ad blockers and iOS ATT (signalbridgedata.com, digitalapplied.com). A test judged on pixel-only data is judged on a partial, biased sample.
- **Server-side conversions recover most of that signal**, typically lifting effective ROAS by a vendor-stated roughly +10-25% over 2-4 weeks as the algorithm adapts (signalbridgedata.com, dataally.ai). Marked vendor-stated; do not treat the recovered lift as a test win, it is a signal-quality change, not a performance change.
- **Match quality matters more than raw event volume.** Sending strong identifiers (hashed email, phone, click ids) drives results more than sending more events with weak matching.
- **Deduplication is a contract.** Browser and server events must pair on a shared key so the same order is not double-counted. A broken dedup setup silently inflates reported conversions and corrupts every downstream measurement.

When you read a result, ask first whether the signal feeding it is complete and well-matched. A confident number built on a leaky, poorly-matched pixel is not evidence.

## Consent is a measurement precondition too

In the EEA, conversion modeling depends on client-side consent signals. If consent is suppressed and no client signal is sent, the conversion is not modeled, it is simply lost. So a drop in reported conversions can reflect a consent or tagging problem rather than a real performance drop. Rule out signal and consent issues before concluding that a change hurt performance. This ties to the GDPR floor: no audience upload without recorded, purpose-appropriate consent (playbook `03`).

## Sources

Statistical floor and spend-per-concept: askneedle.com, zentric.digital. Attribution inflation and iOS signal loss: signalbridgedata.com, digitalapplied.com, lifesight.io, segmentstream.com. Server-side ROAS recovery (roughly +10-25%, vendor-stated): signalbridgedata.com, dataally.ai. Incrementality / holdout power and MMM thresholds (Robyn, Meridian): lifesight.io, incrmntal.com, segmentstream.com.

05-high-aov-funnel.description: Educate-first funnels for high-AOV considered purchases; message match; long windows
05-high-aov-funnel.body:
# High-AOV considered-purchase funnel

Doctrine for advertising expensive products that buyers deliberate over for weeks. A several-hundred-to-thousand-currency-unit product is not an impulse buy: the decision cycle runs weeks, spans many touchpoints, and mixes research, comparison, and trust-building before any purchase (admetrics.io, stackmatix.com). Selling it like a cheap impulse item wastes budget on people who are not ready and never asks for the touchpoints that actually move a considered buyer.

Read this before advising on any funnel for a high-AOV, considered-purchase product.

## Before you advise

1. **Read the account's real spend and volume via tools first** (`account_info` + `insights_query`), and state the regime (see playbook `01`). Funnel shape at a small budget differs from funnel shape at scale: at a small budget you cannot afford broad prospecting AND full-funnel remarketing AND heavy testing at once, so sequencing matters more.
2. **Diagnose where the drop-off actually is before recommending spend.** For these products the upper funnel is frequently strong (good CTR, low CPM at a genuine niche fit) and the gap is the middle of the funnel (initiate-checkout to purchase) plus measurement, NOT attention. Buying more reach when the problem is conversion sets money on fire.

## The considered-purchase reality

- Weeks-long, multi-touch decisions mean a single conversion ad shown cold will underperform. The buyer is not ready to purchase on first contact; they are ready to LEARN. The funnel must offer learning first and the buy ask later.
- These buyers research across many surfaces (reviews, demos, comparison content, peer opinion) before they commit. Your paid funnel is one input among many, so its job is to seed and reinforce the decision, then to close the warm buyer, not to force a cold close.

## Educate-first funnel structure

Lead with education, not a direct-buy ask, when the audience is cold. Structure the funnel in three stages.

### Top / cold: teach and earn a signal

- Serve demo videos, maker or artist content, comparison guides, and mechanism explainers. The goal is to teach and to earn a first-party signal (a video view, a landing-page visit, an email), not to close a sale on first contact.
- Judge this stage on upper-funnel and mid-funnel signals (landing views, email captures), understanding these are directional per playbook `04`, not purchase-tier wins.

### Middle: bridge the consideration gap

- **Lead magnets and email capture** (a buyer's guide, a sign-up incentive, a newsletter) bridge the weeks-long consideration gap and give you a consented first-party audience to remarket to. This is the highest-leverage middle-funnel move for a high-AOV product because it converts anonymous interest into an owned, re-reachable contact.
- Any consent used for a later audience upload must be purpose-appropriate and recorded (the GDPR floor from playbook `03`). A newsletter opt-in that never mentioned ad-platform sharing does NOT cover uploading that list as a custom audience. If the consent basis is unclear, do not upload; flag it.

### Bottom / warm: close on trust

- The conversion ask goes to people who have already engaged, on a window matched to the real decision cycle (below).
- **Trust assets** carry this stage: reviews, endorsements from credible makers or artists, clear warranty and return terms, and visible social proof. For a considered purchase, trust is the conversion lever more than price. Address the buyer's real hesitation (is it good, will it last, can I return it) rather than discounting.
- Sequence the ask: a buyer who watched a full demo and read a comparison guide is a warmer prospect than one who clicked once. Where the platform allows, weight the conversion ask toward the more-engaged segment rather than blasting every past visitor with the same close.

### Why the funnel must be staged, not collapsed

Collapsing all three stages into a single cold conversion campaign is the most common way to waste budget on these products. The cold audience is not ready to buy, so a direct-buy ask to them converts poorly and teaches the delivery system to chase the rare impulsive outlier instead of the typical considered buyer. Staging the funnel lets each ad do the job the buyer is actually ready for at that moment: learn, then consider, then commit.

## Landing-page mechanics for paid traffic

A paid click to a high-AOV product is expensive, so the landing page must convert it rather than leak it.

- **Single call to action.** One clear next step. Multiple competing CTAs split intent and lower conversion.
- **No navigation bar.** Navigation is a set of exits. Remove it on a paid landing page so the only forward path is the CTA.
- **Fast mobile load.** Aim for under three seconds on mobile. Every additional second of load costs roughly 7% of conversions (intensifynow.com), and these buyers often first encounter the product on a phone.
- **Sticky mobile add-to-cart.** Keep the primary action reachable as the buyer scrolls the trust and detail content, so a convinced buyer never has to hunt for the button.
- **Trust above the fold and near the CTA.** Place at least one strong trust signal (a review, an endorsement, a return guarantee) where the buyer sees it while deciding, not buried at the bottom.

## Message match: ad to landing page

Message match is one of the largest controllable CVR levers for these funnels, and it costs nothing but attention.

- The landing-page headline must mirror the ad's promise word for word. A 90%+ match between the ad message and the landing-page message can convert roughly 2.3x better than a match below 60% (intensifynow.com). A mismatch makes the click feel like a bait-and-switch and the buyer bounces.
- Paid landing pages should have a single call to action, no navigation bar to leak attention, a sub-3-second mobile load (every additional second of load costs roughly 7% of conversions), and a sticky mobile add-to-cart.
- If the ad says one thing and the page says another, fix the page or the ad before spending more. No bid change and no audience change recovers a broken message match.

Example of good message match (customer-facing copy):

- Ad: "Play expressive, hands on control for your studio."
- Landing headline: "Expressive, hands on control for your studio." (mirrors the ad, with a single CTA directly below it.)

Note on copy: any customer-facing text you draft in this funnel (ad copy, landing headlines, email subject lines) must avoid dash-style punctuation. Do not use an em dash, an en dash, or a double hyphen as a sentence break. Rewrite with a comma, a colon, or two sentences. For example, write "Free demo inside: see it play" rather than joining the two clauses with a dash.

## Remarketing windows matched to the decision cycle

The single most common misconfiguration on these funnels is a remarketing window that is too short.

- A 7-day remarketing window drops the buyer long before a weeks-long decision cycle closes. Match the window to the real cycle length, typically 30-90 days for a several-hundred-to-thousand-unit product (admetrics.io). A buyer who saw a demo on day two and is ready to buy on day forty must still be in your audience on day forty.
- Read the account's actual time-to-purchase where the data exists rather than guessing; if you cannot measure it, default to a 30-90 day window and say the assumption out loud in your recommendation.
- Retargeting warm audiences converts several times higher and cheaper than cold prospecting, so on small budgets a meaningful slice (roughly a quarter to 40% of budget, per playbook `06` allocation notes) belongs to remarketing, but only against consent-clean, correctly-windowed audiences.

## Budget split for a small high-AOV funnel

At a small budget you cannot fully fund every stage, so allocate deliberately rather than spreading thin.

- Give a meaningful slice (roughly a quarter to 40%) to remarketing, which converts several times higher and cheaper than cold prospecting and is where warm considered buyers actually close (get-ryze.ai, vendor-stated).
- Fund the top of the funnel enough to keep feeding the middle with fresh signals (video views, landing visits, email captures), but do not over-invest in cold reach when the mid-funnel is the bottleneck.
- Let organic and creator content carry brand and education weight the paid budget cannot afford (this ties to playbook `09` on continuity and brand at small budgets). Paid amplifies credibility that content and endorsements create; it rarely manufactures that credibility from scratch.

## Diagnosing the funnel before spending

When asked to improve results, do this in order:

1. Read spend, CTR, CPM, initiate-checkout, and purchase via tools. Confirm whether the gap is attention (rare for these products) or conversion/measurement (common).
2. If upper-funnel is strong and purchases are weak, do NOT buy more reach. Fix message match, the landing page, the trust assets, and the remarketing window first. These are cheap changes with large CVR leverage.
3. Only after the mid-funnel is sound do you scale reach (see playbook `06` for the +20% / 72h scale rule).
4. Throughout, remember that platform-reported purchase values for these funnels can be implausible (playbook `04`); confirm efficiency against first-party revenue and blended MER, not the platform's self-reported number.

## Worked example: improving a stalled high-AOV funnel

Suppose the account shows strong CTR (4-5%) and low CPM but weak purchases.

1. Read CTR, CPM, initiate-checkout, and purchase via tools. The strong CTR and low CPM confirm attention is not the problem; the low purchase count against healthy initiate-checkout points at the mid and bottom of the funnel.
2. Check message match: pull the top ad's promise and the landing-page headline. If they diverge, fix the page to mirror the ad word for word before anything else.
3. Check the remarketing window. If it is 7 days against a weeks-long decision cycle, widen it to 30-90 days so warm buyers are still reachable when they decide.
4. Check trust assets on the landing page: reviews, endorsements, warranty and return clarity, social proof. A considered buyer needs these to commit.
5. Only after message match, window, and trust are sound do you consider adding reach. Confirm any efficiency claim against first-party revenue, not the platform's self-reported purchase value.

## Common questions the doctrine answers

- "Our CTR is great but sales are low, should we spend more on reach?" No. For these products the gap is almost always conversion and measurement, not attention. Fix message match, the landing page, trust assets, and the remarketing window first.
- "Can we upload our newsletter list as a custom audience?" Only if the consent that captured those emails was purpose-appropriate and mentioned ad-platform sharing. A generic newsletter opt-in does not cover it; if unclear, do not upload and flag it (playbook `03`).
- "What remarketing window should we use?" Match it to the real decision-cycle length, typically 30-90 days for a several-hundred-to-thousand-unit product. If you cannot measure the cycle, default to that range and state the assumption.
- "Should we discount to close more sales?" For a considered purchase, trust usually moves the buyer more than price. Strengthen reviews, endorsements, and return clarity before reaching for a discount.

## Trust assets in depth

For a several-hundred-to-thousand-unit product, the buyer's hesitation is rarely price alone; it is risk. Every trust asset reduces a specific risk:

- **Reviews and ratings** reduce the "is it actually good" risk. Real, specific reviews beat generic star counts.
- **Endorsements from credible makers or artists** transfer earned credibility. For niche products, a respected practitioner's word carries more weight than any ad claim, because the audience already trusts that voice. Paid ads amplify this credibility; they do not create it.
- **Warranty and return clarity** reduce the "what if it is wrong for me" risk. State the return path plainly and near the CTA.
- **Visible social proof** (community, usage, named customers) reduces the "am I the only one" risk and signals that a real base of buyers exists.

Order the funnel so these assets reach the buyer during consideration, not only at the final ask. A buyer who has already absorbed the trust signals over a 30-90 day window closes far more readily than one who meets them for the first time at checkout.

## A note on measurement for this funnel

Because these funnels are multi-touch and long, platform attribution is especially unreliable here (playbook `04`): a platform may credit a purchase to the last cheap remarketing impression while ignoring the demo that actually did the convincing. Judge the funnel's health on first-party revenue and blended MER over the full window, not on the platform's per-ad purchase claims. When you report results, state which touchpoints you can and cannot measure honestly.

## Hard rules

1. **Educate first for high-AOV considered purchases.** Do not put direct-buy asks in front of cold audiences; lead with demo, comparison, and trust content, and capture a consented first-party signal to bridge the consideration gap.
2. **Match the ad message to the landing page word for word.** A high message match (90%+) converts far better (roughly 2.3x) than a poor one; fix the page or ad before spending more, since no bid or audience change recovers a broken match.
3. **Match the remarketing window to the real decision-cycle length** (typically 30-90 days for these products), never a default 7-day window; state the assumed cycle length if you cannot measure it.
4. **Any customer-facing example copy in this playbook avoids dash-style punctuation** (no em dash, no en dash, no double hyphen); rewrite with colons, commas, or separate sentences.

## Copy discipline for this funnel

Because this playbook produces customer-facing copy, hold every drafted line to the user-facing surface rule: no dash-style punctuation. Do not use an em dash, an en dash, or a double hyphen as a sentence break in ad copy, landing headlines, email subject lines, or button labels. Rewrite with a colon, a comma, or two separate sentences.

Good and bad patterns:

- Prefer "Expressive control, built for your studio." rather than joining the two clauses with a dash.
- Prefer "Free demo inside: hear it play." rather than a dashed aside.
- Prefer two short sentences over one long dash-spliced sentence: "It is expressive. It is fast."

Keep copy concrete and benefit-led for a considered buyer: name the outcome, mirror the ad promise on the landing page, and let trust assets do the reassurance. Avoid hype adjectives that a skeptical, researching buyer will discount.

## A staged funnel checklist

Before you call a high-AOV funnel healthy, confirm each of these:

1. Cold stage offers learning (demo, comparison, mechanism), not a cold buy ask.
2. A consented email or first-party capture bridges the middle of the funnel.
3. Landing page mirrors the ad message word for word, single CTA, fast mobile load, no nav.
4. Trust assets (reviews, endorsements, warranty, social proof) are visible during consideration.
5. Remarketing window matches the real decision cycle (30-90 days), not 7 days.
6. Efficiency is judged on first-party revenue and blended MER, not platform purchase claims.
7. Any audience upload rests on recorded, purpose-appropriate consent.

If any item fails, fix it before adding reach.

## Sources

Considered-purchase cycle length and educate-first structure: admetrics.io, stackmatix.com. Message match CVR effect and landing-page load impact: intensifynow.com. Retargeting efficiency ranges are vendor-stated (get-ryze.ai) and used only as directional context, not as targets. Lead-magnet and email-bridge tactics: stackmatix.com, convertcart.com.

06-scaling-and-kill-rules.description: Scale +20%/72h, kill vs target CPA, frequency caps, and zombie campaign hygiene
06-scaling-and-kill-rules.body:
# Scaling and kill rules

Codifiable media-buying operations: when to scale a winner, when to kill a loser, how to keep frequency and account hygiene under control. These are the rules that turn a working structure into more spend without breaking the learning system, and that cut waste without cutting things that were merely early.

Read this before you propose any budget increase, pause, or archive.

## Before you act

1. **Read the account's real state via tools first** (`account_info` + `insights_query`): current spend, the configured target CPA if one exists, delivery, frequency, and per-campaign status. Every threshold below is relative to the account's OWN targets and regime, not an absolute (see playbook `01` for the regime taxonomy).
2. **All spend increases are gated.** Propose the change and let the human approve it. Do not raise budgets unilaterally. State the assumed regime and the target the change is measured against so the human can approve on evidence.
3. **Consult open and recent experiments before scaling or killing** (Tier-1 experiment discipline). Do not kill an ad set that is mid-test before its decision date, and do not scale a change whose test result is still inconclusive (playbook `04` owns the decision-date and minimum-sample rules).

## Scaling winners

Scale slowly enough that the learning system keeps up. Fast budget jumps re-trigger the learning phase and throw away the efficiency you built.

- **The rule: +20% every 72 hours on a proven winner. Not faster.** The 72-hour cadence leaves a full attribution window between steps so each increase is judged on settled data, not on noise from the previous change. Expect an account to reach several times its original budget over roughly 90 days while holding ROAS within about 15% of baseline (roaspy.com, adamigo.ai).
- A "winner" is a structure that met its decision date and its minimum sample (playbook `04`), not one that merely looks good after two days. Do not scale on an unconfirmed or upper-funnel-only signal.
- If ROAS or blended MER drifts more than about 15% off baseline as you scale, pause the ramp and hold at the last good budget rather than pushing through the drift.
- Prefer scaling the winning consolidated campaign vertically (raise its budget) over cloning it into many new ad sets. Cloning fragments the learning system and scatters the budget below the significance floor (playbook `01` on consolidation).
- Judge scaling success on first-party revenue and blended MER, not on the platform's self-reported ROAS, which inflates (playbook `04`).

## Killing losers

Kill relative to the account's target CPA, not to a gut feeling and not to an invented number.

- **The rule: pause when CPA exceeds roughly 120% of the target CPA, after the ad set has spent at least about 1x AOV** (theoptimizer.io, scalemate.co). Spending less than 1x AOV before judging is too little data, and killing then is premature; you may be killing a structure that had not yet exited learning.
- A softer variant: if CPA sits above the threshold for two consecutive days, cut that ad set's budget by about 20% rather than killing outright, then re-read on the next window. This lets you de-risk without discarding the learning entirely.
- **If no target CPA is configured on the account, FLAG THE GAP. Do not guess a number.** A kill threshold cannot be set responsibly without a target CPA derived from margin and desired contribution. Tell the human the threshold cannot be set, ask for the target, and hold. Guessing a CPA target silently anchors the account's entire kill discipline to a made-up figure, which is worse than having no rule.
- **Budget floor sanity:** purchase optimization needs a weekly budget of roughly 50x the target CPA to exit learning reliably (get-ryze.ai). Below that floor, optimizing the purchase event directly is starved of conversions; optimize a cheaper, honestly-labeled upstream event instead and say so in the recommendation (this ties directly to the metric tiers in playbook `04`).

## Pause versus budget-cut versus archive

These are three different actions for three different situations; do not conflate them.

- **Pause** an ad set or ad when its CPA clearly breaches the kill threshold after adequate spend, or when it is fatigued past the frequency cap and you want to stop delivery while you prepare a fresh creative. A pause is reversible and preserves the structure.
- **Cut budget by about 20%** when the breach is marginal (for example CPA above the threshold for two consecutive days) and you want to de-risk without discarding the accumulated learning. Re-read on the next window and pause if it worsens.
- **Archive** a campaign that has no ongoing reason to exist: a finished launch, a closed season, or a zombie left ACTIVE for years. Archiving cleans up reporting and removes the risk of accidental re-funding into a cold learning phase.

Pick the lightest action that addresses the actual problem, and always state the target the action is measured against so the human can approve on evidence.

## Frequency caps

Frequency that climbs unchecked burns budget on fatigued audiences and drives CPMs up.

- Cap frequency around 1.5 to 3.0. Above 3.0 you are paying rising CPMs to re-show the same people the same creative, and returns fall (theoptimizer.io, marketkingco.com).
- When frequency approaches the cap, the fix is fresh creative or a broader audience, NOT a higher bid. Rotate the concept (playbook `02`) or widen targeting (playbook `03`). Raising the bid on a fatigued audience just pays more for the same declining response.
- A rising frequency paired with a falling CTR is the fatigue signature; treat that pair as a trigger to refresh, not to spend harder.

## Daily monitoring set

Read these each day and alert on meaningful swings:

- Spend pace, CPA, ROAS or blended MER, CTR, frequency.
- Alert on a day-over-day ROAS swing greater than about 15%, and investigate before reacting. A swing can be attribution noise, especially given the platform inflation and modeling covered in playbook `04`; do not kill or scale on a single noisy day.
- Watch spend pace against budget: an ad set that suddenly spends far faster or slower than its budget usually signals an auction shift or a delivery problem worth reading before acting.
- Pair CTR with frequency: rising frequency plus falling CTR is fatigue; falling CTR at flat frequency is usually a creative or audience-fit problem.

## Why the cadence matters

Every one of these rules exists to protect the delivery system's learning phase. The learning phase is the period during which the platform gathers enough conversions to optimize delivery; it needs settled data and a stable budget. Fast budget jumps, frequent structural edits, and constant new campaigns all reset it, and an account stuck in permanent learning never reaches the efficiency it is capable of. The +20% / 72h scale rule, the 1x-AOV spend gate before killing, and the zombie/churn hygiene are all the same principle in different clothes: give the system stable, settled data to learn from, and change it deliberately rather than reactively.

## Retargeting allocation on small budgets

Retargeting is the highest-efficiency spend on a small account, so protect its share when you scale or cut.

- Warm retargeting audiences convert several times higher and at a materially lower CPA than cold prospecting (get-ryze.ai, vendor-stated ranges). A meaningful slice of a small budget (roughly a quarter to 40%) belongs there.
- When you cut budget under the kill rules, cut from the weakest cold prospecting first, not from working retargeting, unless retargeting itself is the thing breaching the CPA threshold.
- Keep retargeting audiences consent-clean and correctly windowed (playbook `03` for consent, playbook `05` for window length on considered purchases). A cheap conversion against a non-consented audience is not a win; it is a compliance liability.

## Zombie hygiene

Old campaigns left ACTIVE quietly damage the account.

- **Hunt zombie ACTIVE campaigns** with no recent spend or delivery: campaigns left ACTIVE for years after their reason to exist ended (a launch that finished long ago, a season that closed). Archive them. They clutter reporting, confuse allocation reads, and, if accidentally re-funded, restart from a cold learning phase.
- Watch for the churn anti-pattern: an account that has cycled through dozens of short-lived campaigns is stuck in a permanent learning-phase reset, never accumulating the settled data the delivery system needs (playbook `01` on continuity over churn). The fix is to consolidate into a few durable campaigns rather than spinning up a new campaign per idea.
- Beware the cheap-reach trap when auditing awareness spend: an ultra-low-CPM buy that bought hundreds of thousands of impressions at a fraction of a currency unit CPM but produced a near-zero CTR and essentially no landing views is junk placement (low-quality inventory / broad audience-network style placements), not a win. Awareness objectives need placement discipline and a real brand-lift rationale, not CPM bragging rights. A near-zero CTR at a tiny CPM is a signal to cut, not to celebrate the cheap reach.

## Scaling paths: vertical versus horizontal

There are two ways to spend more, and at a small budget one is far safer.

- **Vertical (raise the budget on the winning campaign).** This is the default. It keeps the learning the campaign already accumulated and follows the +20% / 72h cadence. It is the safe path at low volume because it does not fragment the budget.
- **Horizontal (clone the winner into new ad sets or audiences).** This scatters the budget across new cells that each restart in learning and each fall below the significance floor. Avoid it at a small budget. Only reach for horizontal scaling once volume is high enough that new cells can each clear their own learning phase, which a small account rarely can.

When asked to "scale," default to vertical and say why. Reserve horizontal expansion for genuinely new, tested structures funded from the roughly 10-20% testing slice, not as a way to spend a winner's budget faster.

## A worked kill/scale decision

When you evaluate a campaign, walk this order:

1. Is it mid-test before its decision date? If yes, leave it; do not touch it (playbook `04`).
2. Is a target CPA configured? If no, flag the gap and stop; you cannot judge kill/scale responsibly yet.
3. Has it spent at least about 1x AOV? If no, keep gathering data.
4. Is CPA above roughly 120% of target after that spend? If yes, propose a pause (or a 20% budget cut if it is a two-day breach). If no and it is a confirmed winner, propose +20% and set the next review 72 hours out.
5. Is frequency above 3.0? If yes, propose fresh creative or a broader audience regardless of the CPA read.

## Common questions the doctrine answers

- "This campaign is crushing it, can we double the budget today?" No. Scale at +20% every 72 hours. A budget doubling re-triggers the learning phase and discards the efficiency you built.
- "CPA looks high, should I kill it?" Only after it has spent at least about 1x AOV and only relative to the target CPA (pause above roughly 120% of target). If it has spent less than 1x AOV, it may not have exited learning; keep gathering data.
- "There is no target CPA set, what threshold do I use?" None. Flag the gap and ask the human for a target CPA derived from margin and desired contribution. Do not guess a number.
- "Frequency is at 4, should I raise the bid to keep delivery?" No. Above 3.0 the audience is fatiguing; refresh the creative or broaden the audience. A higher bid just pays more for a declining response.
- "There is an old campaign still ACTIVE from a launch two years ago, leave it?" No. Archive it. Zombie ACTIVE campaigns clutter reporting and restart cold if re-funded.
- "This awareness buy got 450k impressions at a tiny CPM, is that a win?" No, if the CTR is near zero and it drove essentially no landing views. That is junk placement, not reach worth having.

## Hard rules

1. **Scale winners at +20% every 72 hours, not faster.** A faster ramp re-triggers the learning phase; hold or back off if ROAS/MER drifts more than about 15% from baseline.
2. **Kill relative to target CPA** (pause when CPA exceeds roughly 120% of target after spending at least about 1x AOV). **If no target CPA is configured, FLAG the gap and ask for one; do not guess a number.**
3. **Cap frequency** around 1.5 to 3.0; above 3.0, fix with fresh creative or a broader audience, never a higher bid.
4. **Hunt zombie ACTIVE campaigns** with no spend or delivery and archive them; avoid the campaign-churn anti-pattern that keeps the account in a permanent learning-phase reset.

## When the account lacks the inputs to decide

Several rules here depend on inputs that may not be configured. Handle the gaps honestly rather than inventing values:

- **No target CPA:** flag it and ask for one; do not guess. This is the single most important gap, because it silently defines all kill discipline.
- **No reliable AOV:** the "spend at least about 1x AOV before judging" gate needs a real AOV. If it is unknown, read it from first-party order data where possible; if you cannot, say the gate cannot be applied precisely and err toward gathering more data before killing.
- **No first-party revenue read:** if you cannot confirm efficiency against first-party revenue, treat platform ROAS as unaudited (playbook `04`) and scale conservatively, stating the limitation.

In every case, the correct move is to surface the missing input to the human, not to substitute a plausible-looking number that quietly becomes the account's operating truth.

## An account-hygiene audit checklist

When asked to review an account's operational health, walk this list and report each finding:

1. **Zombie campaigns:** any ACTIVE campaign with no recent spend or delivery. Recommend archiving.
2. **Churn pattern:** a history of many short-lived campaigns. Recommend consolidating into durable structures (playbook `01`).
3. **Frequency:** any ad set above 3.0. Recommend fresh creative or a broader audience.
4. **Kill threshold configured:** is a target CPA set. If not, flag the gap and ask for one.
5. **Budget floor:** is weekly budget at least roughly 50x the target CPA for purchase optimization. If not, recommend optimizing a cheaper labeled event.
6. **Cheap-reach junk:** any awareness buy with near-zero CTR at a tiny CPM and no landing views. Recommend cutting or fixing placement discipline.
7. **Scaling posture:** are winners being scaled vertically at +20% / 72h, or jumped and cloned. Recommend the disciplined cadence.

Report findings with the specific campaigns or ad sets involved and the target each is measured against, then let the human approve the gated changes.

## Why absolutes are dangerous here

Every threshold in this playbook is relative to the account's own targets and regime. A CPA that is a disaster for one account is healthy for another with different margin. A budget that is generous for one account starves another with a higher target CPA. Always read the account's real figures first and state the regime, then apply these rules as ratios against the account's own targets, never as universal absolute numbers. When the account lacks a target to measure against, the correct output is to surface that gap, not to import a number from elsewhere.

## Sources

Scaling cadence and expected ramp: roaspy.com, adamigo.ai. Kill thresholds and the two-day budget-cut variant: theoptimizer.io, scalemate.co. Purchase-optimization budget floor (roughly 50x target CPA weekly): get-ryze.ai. Frequency caps: theoptimizer.io, marketkingco.com. Retargeting efficiency and cheap-reach observations are vendor-stated or account-observed and used as directional context only.

07-google-specifics.description: Search-platform doctrine, feed-first PMax, brand/non-brand split, negative-keyword governance
07-google-specifics.body:
# Search-platform specifics

Doctrine for the search-and-shopping ad platform (Search, Shopping, and the
consolidated performance product that mixes shopping, search, display, and video
inventory from a single feed plus asset groups). This playbook ships as doctrine
now; the tools for this platform arrive in a later phase. Until they do, apply
these rules when advising, and phrase every read as coming from "the search
platform's <report>" — do NOT invent tool names that do not yet exist in your
toolset. When the tools land, the decision rules here are unchanged.

Before advising on this platform, read the actual account first: current spend,
which campaign types are running, and whether a product feed is connected. State
the assumed budget regime from the real figure (see playbook 01) before making
any structural recommendation. Never assume the budget.

## Feed-first: the feed multiplies everything

For product-led ecommerce the product feed is the single highest-leverage lever
on this platform. Feed completeness and quality gate every downstream result.

Hard rule (a): **the consolidated performance product is feed-first — feed
quality multiplies everything.** "Perfect smart bidding on a 60% complete feed
loses to defaults on a 99% complete feed" (apexdigital.ro, groas.com). A
feed-only configuration (no uploaded creative assets) runs 30-45% lower cost per
sale for product-led ecommerce, because it avoids being pushed into pure-awareness
placements; add creative assets only after you have a feed-driven baseline
(storegrowers.com, digitalapplied.com). So: never try to fix a
feed-quality problem with bid strategy, budget, or creative. Fix the feed first.
The mechanics of diagnosing feed problems are in playbook 08 (merchant feed
health); this playbook covers the campaign structure that sits on top of a
healthy feed.

Decision rule: if a feed-driven campaign is underperforming, check feed health
(playbook 08) BEFORE touching bids, budget, or asset groups. A partial feed
