caps the ceiling no matter what you do above it.

## Brand versus non-brand: always separate

Hard rule (b): **separate brand from non-brand.** Keep branded search (people
typing your name) in its own campaign, separate from non-brand generic search,
for budget, strategy, and reporting. Branded search is cheap, high-intent, and
mostly harvesting demand you already created; non-brand is expensive prospecting.
Blending them lets cheap branded conversions flatter the blended cost per
acquisition and hide non-brand inefficiency.

The consolidated performance product cannibalizes brand terms unless you exclude
them: it will happily spend on your own name and claim credit for conversions
that branded search (or organic) would have captured for far less. Set
brand-term exclusions at the account level (or via the platform rep where the
self-serve UI does not expose them) so the performance product prospects new
demand rather than re-buying your existing demand (storegrowers.com).

Decision rule: if branded and non-brand are in one campaign, or if the
performance product is uncapped on brand terms, flag it. Report the branded
cost per acquisition and the non-brand cost per acquisition SEPARATELY; never
report only the blended figure, which is a misleading average (ties to the
trust-hierarchy doctrine: a blended ratio hides the mix).

## Negative-keyword governance: deliberate, never bulk-blind

Hard rule (c): **govern negative keywords deliberately — bulk negatives silently
suppress delivery.** Negative keywords are how you stop spending on irrelevant
queries, but a careless bulk-negative list (especially broad-match negatives, or
a shared list applied account-wide) can silently block queries you actually want,
and the platform gives no loud warning: delivery just quietly drops. A broad
negative can also block near-variants, plurals, and misspellings you did not
intend.

Governance rules:
- Prefer exact and phrase negatives over broad negatives; a broad negative
  blocks a whole neighborhood of queries.
- Before applying a shared/account-wide negative list, check what converting
  queries it would block. Never apply a large negative list blind.
- Keep a record of why each significant negative was added, so a later reviewer
  can tell an intentional block from an accidental one.
- If delivery drops after a negative-list change, suspect the list first.

Decision rule: never bulk-add negatives without first confirming they do not
overlap converting search terms from the search-terms report.

## Search-terms mining: the continuous hygiene loop

Hard rule (d): **mine the search-terms report continuously.** The search-terms
report shows the actual queries that triggered your ads (as opposed to the
keywords you bid on). It is the ongoing hygiene loop of this platform: harvest
converting queries into their own keywords/asset groups, and negative out the
waste (playbook rule c). This is a recurring cadence, not a one-time setup.

The loop, run on a regular cadence:
1. Read the search platform's search-terms report for the period.
2. Find queries that converted (or show strong intent) but are not yet explicit
   keywords -> promote them.
3. Find queries that spent with no intent/conversion -> add as deliberate
   negatives (rule c: exact/phrase, recorded).
4. Watch for brand-term leakage into non-brand or into the performance product
   (rule b).

At a small budget this matters MORE, not less: a small budget cannot afford to
waste spend on irrelevant queries, and the search-terms report is the cheapest,
highest-signal place to cut waste. At very small budgets on this platform
(roughly <=500-1000/mo), concentrate on 5-10 highest-intent commercial keywords
with exact/phrase focus; broad testing is unaffordable (digitenzy.com, jyll.ca).

## Structure and bidding notes (apply after feed + brand split)

These support the hard rules above; they are not additional hard rules.

- Structure: 3-7 asset groups for the consolidated performance product; the
  platform has expanded search themes substantially, so use themes to steer
  asset groups rather than over-fragmenting (storegrowers.com).
- Bidding ladder: run maximize-conversions / maximize-conversion-value WITHOUT
  targets for the first 2-3 weeks so the platform gathers data, THEN constrain
  with a target cost per acquisition or target return once there is enough
  conversion history (jumpfly.com, modernmarketinginstitute.com). Setting a hard
  target on day one starves a cold campaign of learning data.
- Responsive assets: provide the full complement of headlines and descriptions
  (up to 15 headlines / 5 descriptions per responsive search ad); more quality
  assets give the platform more combinations to assemble (jumpfly.com). This is
  asset breadth, not creative testing — creative testing doctrine is playbook 02.
- Statistical honesty still applies: at low purchase volume, conversion-based
  optimization and targets will be noisy. Treat click-through and cost-per-click
  movements as directional only, set decision dates, and do not declare a keyword
  or asset-group "winner" on upper-funnel signal alone (see playbook 04).

## Interaction with other playbooks

- Feed diagnosis and repair: playbook 08 (merchant feed health).
- Budget regime and whether this platform belongs in the mix at the current
  budget: playbook 01 (account structure) and playbook 09 (budget allocation).
- Metric tiers, minimum samples, and decision dates: playbook 04.
- Trust hierarchy for cross-platform numbers (never compare this platform's
  reported conversions against another platform's — each claims the same orders):
  see the always-on doctrine and playbook 04.

## Hard rules recap

- (a) The consolidated performance product is feed-first: feed quality
  multiplies everything. Fix the feed before bids/budget/creative.
- (b) Separate brand from non-brand for budget, strategy, and reporting; exclude
  brand terms from the performance product; report the two cost-per-acquisition
  figures separately.
- (c) Govern negative keywords deliberately: bulk/broad negatives silently
  suppress delivery. Prefer exact/phrase, check overlap first, record intent.
- (d) Mine the search-terms report continuously: promote converters, negative
  out waste, watch for brand leakage.

08-merchant-feed-health.description: Merchant feed health: fix product-data issues in the store, route non-data issues manually
08-merchant-feed-health.body:
# Merchant feed health

Doctrine for keeping the product feed that powers the search-and-shopping
platform's shopping and consolidated-performance campaigns healthy. This playbook
ships as doctrine now; the merchant tools arrive in a later phase. Until they do,
apply these rules when advising, and phrase every read as coming from "the
merchant platform's issue/diagnostics report" — do NOT invent tool names that do
not yet exist in your toolset. The classification and routing rules here are
unchanged once the tools land.

Read the account first. Before advising on feed problems, confirm which
campaigns depend on the feed and what the merchant platform is currently
reporting. State the assumed budget regime (playbook 01) before recommending
structural work.

## Why this matters: feed quality gates all delivery

Hard rule (c): **feed quality gates all delivery on the search-and-shopping
platform.** A product with a disapproved or incomplete feed entry does not serve,
no matter how much budget or how good the bid strategy. This is the same
feed-first principle as playbook 07 (a 99%-complete feed on default bidding beats
a 60%-complete feed on perfect bidding), viewed from the feed side. Disapprovals
and warnings on the feed are therefore the FIRST thing to check when
shopping/performance delivery is low or a product is not showing.

Decision rule: if shopping or feed-driven performance delivery is low, read the
merchant platform's issue report BEFORE touching bids, budget, or campaign
structure. A suppressed feed cannot be fixed above the feed.

## Issue taxonomy: two fundamentally different classes

Every merchant-platform issue falls into one of two classes, and they route
completely differently. Classifying correctly is the core of this playbook.

**Class 1 — product-data issues.** The product's own data in the feed is wrong,
missing, or stale. Examples: missing or mismatched GTIN/identifier, missing
brand, price mismatch between feed and landing page, availability mismatch
(feed says in stock, page says sold out), missing or too-small image, missing
required attribute (color/size/condition), title/description quality, currency
mismatch. These originate in the product record and flow into the feed.

**Class 2 — non-product-data issues.** The problem is NOT in the product record.
Examples: landing-page/website problems (page unreachable, content-policy issues
on the page, crawlability), shipping and tax settings at the account level,
business/domain verification, account-level policy or misrepresentation flags,
returns-policy configuration. These are account, site, or policy configuration,
not fields you edit on a product.

## Routing Class 1: fix in the store, concretely

Hard rule (a): **product-data issues route to concrete store product edits.**
When a Class-1 issue is identified, the resolution is a specific, named edit to
the product record in the store (the same store that syncs the feed). Do not
describe the fix abstractly; name the field and the corrective value.

Procedure:
1. Read the merchant platform's issue report; for each issue, identify the
   affected product(s) and the exact attribute at fault.
2. Confirm it is Class 1 (a field on the product record).
3. Specify the concrete store edit: which product, which field, what the correct
   value is (e.g. "set availability to in stock to match the live page", "add a
   GTIN", "correct the feed price to match the landing-page price of X",
   "replace the image with one at least the minimum required dimensions").
4. After the store edit and the next feed sync, re-check the issue report to
   confirm the disapproval cleared. Feed changes are not instant; allow the sync
   and re-crawl before concluding the fix failed.

Price and availability mismatches are the most common and most damaging Class-1
issues: the platform cross-checks the feed against the live landing page, so the
real fix is to make the feed and the page agree. If they disagree because the
page is right and the feed is stale, fix the feed source (the store product);
if the page is wrong, that edges into Class 2 (landing page).

## Routing Class 2: name the action, take no tool path

Hard rule (b): **non-product-data issues are informational only — name the
merchant platform's recommended action, give NO tool path, and make NO merchant
write.** These issues cannot be fixed by editing a product field, and the correct
resolution lives in account settings, the website, business verification, or a
policy review that a human must perform. Your job is to CLASSIFY and REPORT, not
to act.

For a Class-2 issue:
1. Identify the issue class (landing page, shipping/tax settings, business/domain
   verification, policy/misrepresentation, returns policy, etc.).
2. State the merchant platform's own recommended action in plain terms
   (e.g. "complete domain verification in the merchant account", "configure
   shipping settings for the target country", "the landing page must be reachable
   and match policy", "submit the account for policy re-review after correcting
   the flagged content").
3. Explicitly note this is informational: there is no automated tool path here
   and no merchant write should be attempted. Route it to a human for the
   settings/site/policy change.
4. Do NOT guess account-level settings or attempt to auto-resolve a policy flag.

Never attempt a merchant-side write to resolve a Class-2 issue even once the
merchant tools exist. The write surface is for product-data corrections routed
through the store; account/site/policy configuration is a human, out-of-band
action.

## Prioritization

When multiple issues are present, prioritize by delivery impact:
- Account-level suppressions (business verification incomplete, account-level
  policy flag) can suppress the ENTIRE feed — surface these first even though
  they are Class 2 and human-routed, because nothing else matters until they
  clear.
- Then Class-1 disapprovals on high-value or best-selling products.
- Then warnings that degrade ranking/competitiveness but do not suppress.

Report the impact honestly: "these N products are fully suppressed" is a
different severity from "these have quality warnings but still serve".

## Common Class-1 fixes at a glance

A quick-reference mapping from frequent product-data issues to the concrete store
edit. Each is a field on the product record; each re-checks after the next sync.

- Missing/invalid product identifier -> add the correct GTIN/identifier (or set
  identifier-exists correctly for products that legitimately have none).
- Missing brand -> populate the brand field on the product.
- Price mismatch (feed vs live page) -> correct the feed price so it matches the
  landing page; the platform cross-checks the two.
- Availability mismatch -> set availability to match the live page's true stock
  state.
- Image too small / missing -> replace with an image at least the required
  minimum dimensions.
- Missing required attribute (color/size/condition) -> populate the missing
  attribute for the affected variants.
- Currency mismatch -> correct the feed currency to the target market's currency.

If an item on the issue report is NOT reducible to one of these product-field
edits, it is almost certainly Class 2 — route it per hard rule (b).

## Statistical and reporting honesty

Feed health is largely deterministic (a product is approved or it is not), so it
is a rare place where you can speak in near-certainties rather than the
directional language required for performance metrics. Still, do not overclaim a
delivery recovery from a feed fix until the next sync + re-crawl has actually
cleared the issue and delivery has resumed — report the fix as "applied, pending
re-approval" until confirmed.

## Interaction with other playbooks

- Campaign structure on top of a healthy feed, brand/non-brand split,
  negative-keyword governance, search-terms mining: playbook 07.
- Whether the search-and-shopping platform belongs in the budget mix at all at
  the current regime: playbook 01 and playbook 09.
- Metric honesty for anything downstream of delivery: playbook 04.

## Hard rules recap

- (a) Product-data (Class-1) issues route to concrete, named store product
  edits (field + correct value); re-check after the feed sync.
- (b) Non-product-data (Class-2) issues are informational: name the merchant
  platform's recommended action, give NO tool path, make NO merchant write,
  route to a human.
- (c) Feed quality gates all delivery on the search-and-shopping platform: check
  the feed issue report before touching bids, budget, or structure.

09-budget-allocation-brand-activation.description: Cross-platform budget allocation and brand vs activation balance at small budgets
09-budget-allocation-brand-activation.body:
# Budget allocation and brand/activation balance

Doctrine for splitting budget across platforms and between brand-building and
activation (direct-response). This playbook is platform-neutral: apply it to
whichever ad platforms are actually in the mix. Read the real spend first, state
the assumed budget regime (playbook 01) from the actual monthly figure, and only
then allocate. Never assume the budget; never propose a split without first
reading what is being spent and where.

## Read before you allocate

Before any allocation recommendation:
1. Read the account's actual monthly spend and how it is currently distributed
   across platforms and objectives (via the platform read tools).
2. Determine the budget regime (playbook 01: small <5k/mo, mid, larger).
3. State the regime explicitly, then apply the rules below scaled to that regime.

The strategic frames in this playbook come from brand-science research done at
large-brand scale. At a small budget they are DIRECTIONS, not literal splits.
Applying a big-brand ratio mechanically to a tiny budget is a common and
expensive mistake.

## Strategic frames: use as direction, not literal split

Hard rule (a): **treat the 95:5 and 60:40 frames as strategic FRAMES, not literal
splits at small budgets.**

- **95:5 (Ehrenberg-Bass):** at any given moment roughly 95% of category buyers
  are NOT in-market; performance/activation ads harvest the ~5% who are buying
  now, while brand building determines whose shortlist the other 95% carry when
  they eventually enter the market (marketingscience.info, John Dawes). The
  lesson is that most of your future buyers are not ready today, so pure
  bottom-funnel harvesting has a hard ceiling — it can only ever capture the
  current 5%.
- **60:40 (Binet & Field):** across long-run studies, roughly 60% brand-building
  to 40% activation is the effectiveness optimum for sustained growth; for B2B,
  brand-science evidence argues for an even more brand-weighted mix
  (mi-3.com.au, marketingarchitects.com).

Do NOT read these as "spend 60% of a 1.5k/mo budget on brand ads." At small
budgets a literal 60% brand split buys too little reach on any single channel to
build mental availability, while starving the activation that pays the bills. The
frames tell you which DIRECTION to lean and why continuity matters (rule b); they
do not set the arithmetic. Translate them into the small-budget actions below.

## Continuity beats bursts at small budgets

Hard rule (b): **at small budgets, continuity beats bursts.** The actionable
translation of the brand frames for a niche brand on a modest budget is:
always-on, modest, continuous spend beats seasonal blasts. Continuous presence is
how you build mental availability and category-entry-point associations you can
afford; it also protects the learning phase (playbook 01) that repeated on/off
campaign churn destroys. A pattern of many short-lived campaigns is a permanent
learning-phase reset and an anti-pattern (zombie/churn hygiene: playbook 06).

Practical small-budget allocation:
- Run a small number of consolidated, continuously-running campaigns (playbook
  01) rather than turning campaigns on and off by season.
- Carry the brand layer largely through organic and creator/earned content,
  which a small paid budget cannot fund at reach; let paid focus on activation
  plus the modest always-on presence that continuity requires. (Creator-borne
  credibility is amplified by paid, rarely created by it.)
- Where budget genuinely does not stretch to a real brand-building presence, say
  so honestly and lean the paid budget toward efficient activation while the
  brand layer rides on organic — do not pretend a tiny brand-ad line is building
  meaningful mental availability.

## Blended MER cannot justify cutting brand or continuity

Hard rule (c): **blended MER cannot by itself justify cutting brand or continuity
budget.** Blended marketing-efficiency ratio (total real revenue / total ad
spend across all channels) is the operating efficiency truth and outranks any
single platform's self-reported return — but it is a rear-view, DIRECTIONAL
efficiency ratio, not an incrementality measure. It cannot separate demand you
CREATED from demand you merely CAPTURED. Brand building and continuity mostly
create future demand; their payoff shows up later and diffusely, exactly where a
blended ratio is blind.

So when someone points at blended MER to argue for cutting brand or continuity
spend and reallocating everything to the highest-attributed activation channel:
refuse that inference. Cutting brand/continuity often flatters blended MER in the
short term (you stop paying for the slow-burn layer while still harvesting the
demand it already seeded) and erodes the demand pipeline underneath. This ties
directly to the always-on trust-hierarchy doctrine: MER is directional, not
incrementality; only a real incrementality test (a holdout, when volume permits —
playbook 04) can adjudicate whether brand/continuity spend is incremental, and at
small volume that test is usually underpowered, so structural judgment governs,
not the ratio.

Decision rule: never recommend cutting brand/continuity budget on the strength of
blended MER (or any platform ROAS) alone. Require an incrementality signal, or
state plainly that it cannot be measured at this volume and the decision is a
judgment call, not a data-driven one.

## Reach over frequency where budget allows

Hard rule (d): **prefer reach over frequency where budget allows.** Mental
availability is built by reaching MORE distinct category buyers, not by hitting
the same small audience repeatedly. Excessive frequency on a small audience wastes
budget and drives fatigue: keep frequency capped in the roughly 1.5-3.0 range;
above ~3 you get fatigue and rising CPMs, and should refresh creative or broaden
rather than keep paying to re-hit the same people (theoptimizer.io,
marketkingco.com). Where budget allows a choice, spend the marginal unit on
broader reach rather than higher frequency on an already-covered audience.

Caveat: this is "where budget allows." At the smallest budgets, retargeting a
warm, already-reached audience converts far more efficiently, so a portion of a
small budget still belongs on efficient activation/retargeting; the reach-over-
frequency rule governs the PROSPECTING/brand portion, not the retargeting portion.

## Cross-platform allocation

When more than one platform is in the mix:
- Do NOT compare platforms on their own self-reported return to decide the split
  — each platform claims the same orders and grades its own homework (always-on
  trust hierarchy; playbook 04). Use blended MER (DTC-split; see below) and
  structural judgment.
- Match platform to intent: a search-and-shopping platform harvests existing
  demand (high intent, closer to the 5%); a social/discovery platform creates and
  reaches demand (closer to the 95%). A healthy mix usually needs both a harvest
  channel and a demand-creation/reach channel; do not put the entire small budget
  on one and declare the other "worse" using unaudited platform numbers.
- Concentrate rather than fragment: at a small budget, spreading thinly across
  many platforms leaves every one below the volume it needs to exit learning and
  to measure anything (playbook 01). Fewer platforms, run continuously, beats many
  run thinly.

DTC/wholesale split: before drawing any allocation conclusion from revenue,
split out B2B/wholesale revenue from direct-to-consumer. B2B demand-sensing is
coarse and must never sit in a conversion feed; do not let wholesale revenue
inflate the blended MER you are using to allocate consumer ad budget.

## Interaction with other playbooks

- Regime definition and consolidation at small budgets: playbook 01.
- Learning-phase protection and continuity vs churn: playbook 01; zombie/churn
  hygiene: playbook 06.
- Blended MER, incrementality, holdouts, and metric honesty: playbook 04 and the
  always-on trust-hierarchy doctrine.
- The search-and-shopping platform's role in the mix: playbook 07.

## Hard rules recap

- (a) 95:5 (Ehrenberg-Bass) and 60:40 (Binet & Field) are strategic FRAMES, not
  literal splits at small budgets.
- (b) At small budgets, continuity (always-on modest spend) beats seasonal
  bursts.
- (c) Blended MER cannot by itself justify cutting brand/continuity budget (it is
  directional, not incrementality) — ties to the trust hierarchy.
- (d) Prefer reach over frequency where budget allows (cap frequency ~1.5-3.0;
  above ~3 refresh or broaden).
